title: ETag
explain: An ETag is a version tag for a resource: a string the server returns that changes whenever the content changes. It can be a plain version number or, more commonly, a signature such as a content hash. I use it for cache revalidation, so an unchanged resource costs a tiny 304 instead of a full download, and for optimistic concurrency on writes.
model:
ETag is, simply put, a version number; very often it is the resource's signature, so "same tag" means "same content".

```
GET /report            -> 200  ETag: "v7"   (body)
...cached copy goes stale...
GET /report
If-None-Match: "v7"    -> 304 Not Modified  (no body)   # still v7: reuse your copy
                       -> 200  ETag: "v8"   (new body)  # changed
```

- **Revalidation:** saves bandwidth and transfer time, not the round trip. To skip the round trip the response must still be fresh (`max-age`; see [client-side caching](#/sd/f/client-side-cache)).
- **Cheap tags:** derive from a stored row version or `updated_at` so the server can answer 304 before rendering anything. Multiple servers must emit the **same tag for the same content** (a content hash, not an inode or timestamp).
- **Optimistic concurrency:** `PUT` with `If-Match: "v3"`; if the current version is no longer v3 the server returns `412 Precondition Failed`, preventing lost updates.
- **Strong vs weak:** `"abc"` means byte-identical; `W/"abc"` means semantically equivalent.

details.q: What does a 304 save compared with a 200?
details.a: The response body only. The request and response still make the round trip. To avoid the round trip the cached response must still be fresh, so the client does not ask at all.

details.q: Why is hashing the whole body a poor way to compute an ETag for an expensive endpoint?
details.a: You must render the body to hash it, so a 400 ms report still costs 400 ms even when the answer is 304. Derive the tag from a stored row version, updated_at or a counter and check it before rendering.

details.q: Why must servers behind a load balancer produce identical ETags?
details.a: Otherwise a client revalidating against a different server sees a different tag for the same content and gets a full 200. Use a content hash or stored version, not inode numbers or file timestamps that differ per machine.

details.q: How does If-Match prevent lost updates?
details.a: Editor A and B both load version v3. A saves with If-Match v3 and succeeds, moving it to v4. B's save with If-Match v3 now fails with 412, so B must refetch and merge instead of silently overwriting A.

details.q: How much does ETag polling save? Take 10,000 clients polling a 2 MB resource every 30 s, 99% unchanged.
details.a: Polls are about 333/s. With ETags only 1% return the body: 3.33 x 2 MB, about 6.7 MB/s. Without them every poll returns it: about 667 MB/s, a 100x difference.

A strong tag promises byte-for-byte identity and is needed for range requests. A weak tag (W/"...") promises only semantic equivalence, which is enough for page caching when, say, compression or whitespace may differ.

prompts.q: Explain ETags to an interviewer and describe a conditional GET.
points: A version tag or content signature for a representation
Server returns it in the ETag header
Client sends If-None-Match when the copy is stale
Unchanged: 304 with no body; changed: 200 with new tag

prompts.q: Besides caching, how else is an ETag useful?
points: Cheap change detection for polling or sync

prompts.q: Design ETag generation for a heavy report endpoint behind several servers.
points: Tag from a stored version or updated_at, not from the rendered body
Check the tag before rendering to answer 304 cheaply
Same content gives the same tag on every server
